## Nivedita Bhadra

**Senior Computational Scientist** working at the intersection of physics, statistical modeling, and biomedical data.

I trained as a physicist, then carried that quantitative foundation into biomedical research and statistical genetics — building models that have to hold up against real, messy, large-scale data.

I'm currently at the **Institute of Biological Psychiatry, Denmark**, where I build statistical genetics models for risk prediction on large-scale cohort data — liability-scale modeling, polygenic risk scores, and related quantitative genetics methods.

Before that, I spent several years at the **Translational Genomics Research Institute (TGen)**, applying high-dimensional statistical modeling to biomedical and clinical data.

My path into this work started in physics: an M.Sc. from IIT Delhi, followed by a PhD in Computational Physics from IISER Kolkata, where I built numerical models of complex physical systems. That grounding in simulation, statistical inference, and large-scale computation is the thread connecting everything since — whether the system is physical, genomic, or textual.

My core focus is population genomics and statistical genetics. I compute polygenic risk scores at scale using SBayesR via GCTB — including a large-scale analysis of iPSYCH2015 (N=105,477) that generated roughly 10,000 PGS from FinnGen and UK Biobank summary statistics. I also work on causal inference in pharmacogenomics, using genetic variants as instruments in Mendelian randomization, and I've built Martingale residual transformations to convert Cox models into linear GWAS.

Outside genomics, I apply predictive modeling — LASSO, random forest, XGBoost, ensemble and Super Learner methods — to clinical trial and biomedical data. I've also worked with phylogenetic comparative methods (PGLS, MDMR), leading transcriptome-lifespan association analyses across species while controlling for phylogenetic non-independence.

Day to day, I work in Python, R, and SQL. I use scikit-learn and XGBoost for predictive modeling, and Hugging Face's pipeline API — BERT, DistilBERT, Sentence-BERT, BERTopic — with PyTorch for GPU-accelerated inference on HPC systems. I build reproducible pipelines with Snakemake, Docker, and Singularity on Linux/HPC, and I've built and deployed end-to-end ML pipelines, from model training through FastAPI, documented in technical write-ups on Medium.
